title: An end-to-end superpolynomial quantum speedup on large classical data

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a quantum computation that solves a specified family of problems involving large classical datasets with a superpolynomial resource advantage over the strongest applicable classical alternatives, after counting the entire workflow. Preparing and loading the input, accessing it during computation, managing errors, performing classical control and extracting the requested answer must all enter the comparison. An algorithm that makes very few queries to an assumed free data oracle would not, by itself, achieve this goal.

A major proposed enabling technology is quantum random-access memory, or QRAM: memory that a quantum processor can address in a superposition of locations while preserving the coherence needed by its algorithm. For algorithms that operate on large stored databases, the challenge is to make this access physically reliable and sufficiently economical that its implementation does not consume the apparent algorithmic advantage. QRAM is not the only possible input mechanism; when data entries can be computed efficiently, a circuit may provide the required access without a physical QRAM database.

The concept therefore combines an input mechanism, a suitable quantum algorithm and a defensible classical comparison. Efficient memory alone is insufficient. Classical algorithms may exploit the same data structures and sampling access used to prepare quantum inputs, substantially narrowing an apparent separation. The intended achievement is an advantage that survives these comparisons for a clearly defined task, rather than a general promise that quantum computers will accelerate arbitrary large datasets.

significance.text: Conditional on success, the direct breakthrough would be a superpolynomial reduction in the specified resource measure for a demonstrated family of classical-data problems, including input preparation and requested-output extraction. This would substantially expand the established practical scope of quantum computation by showing that an advantage can survive the costs of handling large external datasets. The resource claim must identify whether the separation concerns runtime, energy, hardware–time cost or another explicit measure.

The motivating distinction from compact-input applications is useful but limited. Factoring begins with a compact integer, whereas database-based quantum linear algebra can require access to many stored entries. Quantum simulation also concerns a different input setting from processing an arbitrary classical database. These distinctions explain why large-data access deserves its own breakthrough criterion; they do not establish that every scientific problem has a large input or that every classical-data quantum algorithm needs QRAM.

Potential applications include selected linear-algebra and classical-data learning problems, with high-dimensional scientific computing a further conditional possibility. Extending a successful demonstration to broad portions of these fields would require additional suitable algorithms, favorable input structure, acceptable accuracy and affordable outputs. Efficient coherent memory does not automatically confer an advantage across the bulk of linear algebra, scientific computing or machine learning. New scientific discoveries would require subsequent application and validation work.

Tang’s recommendation-systems result illustrates why the comparison matters: a prominent proposed exponential machine-learning advantage disappeared when a classical algorithm received comparable sampling access. That result narrows one application claim rather than ruling out the broader innovation. Likewise, critiques of existing QRAM designs establish serious obstacles without proving that all future architectures or input mechanisms must fail.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unresolved capability is a complete memory-and-algorithm implementation whose advantage survives physical resource accounting and strong classical competition. For large, unstructured stored datasets, a central engineering barrier is coherent access that remains economical after loading, access circuitry, classical control, error management and output extraction are included. The requirement is an overall advantage in stated resources; it does not require storage space, time and energy each independently to scale better than a classical scan.

Jaques and Rattew distinguish active QRAM, with control effort involved in operating the access network, from passive proposals intended to avoid that cost. Their analysis finds that active implementations can lose most asymptotic quantum-linear-algebra advantage once an appropriately resourced parallel classical alternative is considered. Passive approaches face physical implementation and scalability obstacles. These conclusions concern the models and proposals examined, with architectural qualifications; they are not a general impossibility theorem.

Error resilience also needs to become scalable error management. Favorable noise scaling in bucket-brigade QRAM does not alone establish fault tolerance at arbitrarily large sizes: the survey notes that overall QRAM error cannot fall below the underlying physical error rates in the analysis discussed. A device would need to preserve useful coherent access at the scale and accuracy its algorithm requires, including the cost of whatever protection supplies that reliability.

Algorithmic barriers remain even if memory access improves. Theoretical quantum linear-system algorithms such as Harrow–Hassidim–Lloyd already exist, but their existence does not establish a complete large-data advantage. A successful application must meet its input assumptions, deliver the specified output at matched accuracy and success probability, and retain a separation from classical algorithms with comparable access. Tang’s result shows that sampling-based classical methods can be decisive in this last step. The obstacles therefore extend beyond hardware cost alone.

current_state.text: Quantum linear-system algorithms are established theoretical starting points. Tang’s paper traces this line of work to Harrow, Hassidim and Lloyd’s 2008 algorithm. This is an algorithmic achievement, not evidence that a fault-tolerant implementation has demonstrated the end-to-end large-classical-data speedup defined here.

Ewin Tang’s “A quantum-inspired classical algorithm for recommendation systems,” with arXiv version 3 revised on 9 May 2019 and a STOC 2019 conference version, provides a concrete dequantization result. Under the relevant low-rank and sampling-access assumptions, the classical algorithm is only polynomially slower than the Kerenidis–Prakash quantum recommendation algorithm and can use the same input data structure. Consequently, that particular quantum algorithm does not supply the previously claimed exponential separation. This conclusion does not extend automatically to every quantum learning algorithm or dataset.

In the supplied version of “QRAM: A Survey and Critique,” dated 9 November 2025, Samuel Jaques and Arthur G. Rattew report that every non-circuit QRAM proposal they found falls short in at least one respect. They also find that active QRAM can erase most asymptotic advantage in the quantum-linear-algebra models examined. Their discussion of bucket-brigade errors separates favorable noise resilience from fault tolerance at arbitrary scale, while leaving room for possible practical advantages from noisy QRAM at realistic sizes. The authors do not prove the obstacles inevitable.

The supplied survey text ends during Section 8.1, before the detailed hardware critiques in Sections 9–10. Its overall conclusion can therefore be attributed to the authors, but the supplied review does not independently assess every examined design. Tang’s supplied PDF extraction covers all 32 pages, although the review notes some extraction defects. These access limits constrain the detail that can be established from the available material; they do not show that the underlying results are false.

The supplied evidence does not establish an achieved end-to-end superpolynomial advantage of this kind. It also does not establish a current global inventory of QRAM hardware as of 1 November 2026: no substantive freshness update accompanies the dated sources, and “meaningful size” has no specified threshold. The earlier categorical claim that no meaningful fault-tolerant QRAM exists should therefore remain an open hardware-status question. Physical feasibility is uncertain, rather than demonstrated impossible.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: pre-register a family of sparse linear systems, high-dimensional differential equations or classical-data learning tasks, and test input sizes growing by successive powers of two. These are proposed benchmark options, not applications all established by the supplied sources or an accepted completion standard. Define the requested output, accuracy, success probability, input representation, data structure, update pattern and any reuse of preprocessing before making the comparison.
completion_criteria.label: Fully specified pre-registered family tested at successive powers of two

completion_criteria.text: Proposed resource accounting: report complete runtime, energy and hardware requirements, including preparation and loading of the classical data, access operations, classical control, error correction and output extraction. State the number of uses over which loading or preprocessing is amortized, and distinguish initial setup from repeated-query performance. Identify the resource ratio claimed to be superpolynomial; faster runtime accompanied by greater hardware expenditure must be made explicit rather than hidden inside an oracle assumption.
completion_criteria.label: Full resource costs, amortization, and claimed superpolynomial ratio reported

completion_criteria.text: The classical comparison should use the strongest applicable parallel algorithms under explicit, comparable data-access and hardware-budget assumptions. Include ℓ²-norm sampling when the input preparation or data structure supplies comparable classical sampling access. Tang’s result motivates this requirement without implying that every quantum algorithm can be dequantized. A free-oracle query advantage, or a separation that disappears under the matched classical comparison, would not meet this proposed end-to-end criterion.
completion_criteria.label: Advantage over strongest parallel algorithms under matched access and hardware

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidence for scaling and reproducibility: combine measurements with an explicit asymptotic resource analysis that includes physical access and error-management costs. Make benchmark instances, implementations, correctness checks and resource-accounting assumptions available for independent reproduction. Measurements at finitely many doubled sizes establish performance across that tested range; they cannot alone prove superpolynomial scaling or universal advantage.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible measurements plus asymptotic physical access and error-management costs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: report the demonstrated dataset sizes, error rates, output requirements, hardware scale and crossover range, and explain which changes in data structure, accuracy or update frequency remove the advantage. A convincing result may apply to a restricted problem family. Its scope should be stated precisely, with broader scientific or industrial applications treated as subsequent demonstrations.
completion_criteria.label: Precise statement of demonstrated limits and advantage-removing conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: QUA-01, “Distance-scalable universal fault-tolerant quantum computation,” and QUA-08, “Local, universal fault tolerance whose overhead stays bounded as the error falls,” concern reliable computation and its overhead. Both could enable QUA-09, whose defining additional requirement is an end-to-end advantage on large classical data. Neither reliable universality nor favorable error-correction overhead alone resolves input access, output costs or classical competition.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-04, “A laboratory material that stores a logical qubit passively at nonzero temperature,” concerns passive preservation of quantum information. Such storage is distinct from coherently addressing a large database. QUA-05, “Universal computation by braiding non-Abelian anyons,” and QUA-10, “Foundry-made fault-tolerant quantum computation without a dilution refrigerator,” describe possible physical routes to computation. Success in any of these concepts would not by itself demonstrate QUA-09’s application-level resource separation.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-06, “Fault-tolerant quantum interconnects that let processors scale by adding modules,” could help provide the hardware scale needed for a large-data implementation. Modular connectivity and coherent database access remain distinct capabilities. Any interconnect costs incurred by a QUA-09 implementation would belong in its end-to-end accounting.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-02, “Cryptographically relevant execution of Shor’s algorithm,” is a specific compact-input application milestone. QUA-03, “Experimentally confirmed quantum prediction of sign-problematic matter,” is a scientific prediction and validation milestone. QUA-09 instead centers on the resource cost of processing large classical inputs. These milestones may share hardware and algorithms, but demonstrating one would not establish either of the others.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-07, “A proof that quantum polynomial time exceeds classical polynomial time on decision problems,” is a mathematical separation between computational classes. QUA-09 is an implementation and resource-accounting goal for a specified problem family, potentially involving sampling or numerical outputs rather than decision answers. Finite experimental evidence for QUA-09 would not prove QUA-07, and a proof of QUA-07 would not supply economical memory or a practical large-data implementation.

Classical-data quantum machine learning is an overlapping application area within QUA-09, especially where it uses quantum linear algebra and database access. It does not require a separate missing principle here, although particular algorithms can have different input mechanisms and some can use efficiently computable entries without physical QRAM. Tang’s recommendation-systems result is a specific caution about matched-access classical algorithms, not grounds for deleting the broader application area.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish the state or scale of fault-tolerant QRAM hardware as of 1 November 2026. A quantitative definition of useful size is also missing.
The survey extraction stops during Section 8.1, so the supplied review cannot independently assess the detailed hardware critiques in Sections 9–10.
No specific benchmark family, requested output, accuracy target, resource metric or classical hardware budget has been selected for a completion demonstration.

It remains open whether an architecture and algorithm can preserve a superpolynomial end-to-end advantage after coherent access, error management, classical parallelism and applicable dequantization are included.
The physical obstacles identified for existing QRAM proposals are not proven inevitable; the supplied evidence resolves neither general feasibility nor general impossibility.

brief.title: Vastly more efficient computing on large datasets
possible: Researchers could solve a defined family of problems on large datasets with a quantum computer whose advantage grows faster than any fixed power of dataset size. That advantage would survive counting the whole job, from loading the data to extracting the answer.
why: This would expand what quantum computing can usefully tackle. Researchers working on selected calculations with many linked equations or learning from classical data could benefit from savings that survive the cost of handling their datasets.

sources.who: Samuel Jaques and Arthur G. Rattew
sources.showed: They analyzed quantum random-access memory, which lets a quantum computer address multiple memory locations in a quantum state. In the models examined, operating its controls can consume most of the claimed advantage over ordinary computers working in parallel.
sources.quote: We apply these arguments in detail to quantum linear algebra and prove that most asymptotic quantum advantage disappears with active QRAM systems, with some nuance related to the architectural assumptions.
sources.cited_for: The physical cost of accessing data can erase an algorithm’s apparent advantage.
sources.not_established: Their analysis neither demonstrates an economical, scalable memory system nor proves that every future design must fail.

sources.showed: Tang developed an ordinary-computer recommendation algorithm that removed a proposed exponential quantum advantage. It relies on strong assumptions about the data and comparable access to samples from it.
sources.quote:
As a
consequence, Kerenidis and Prakash’s algorithm does not in fact give an exponential
speedup over classical algorithms.
sources.cited_for: A fair comparison must let ordinary algorithms exploit the data access used to prepare quantum inputs.
sources.not_established: This result addresses a particular recommendation task; it does not rule out advantages for all quantum learning algorithms.

shown: Harrow, Hassidim and Lloyd developed a theoretical quantum algorithm for solving systems of linear equations. Such algorithms provide a starting point, but they do not demonstrate the required advantage for a complete computation on a large stored dataset.
missing: A complete implementation must retain its advantage after data loading, control, error management and answer extraction are counted.
Data access must remain reliable and affordable at the scale the algorithm needs.
A suitable task must retain its advantage against the strongest ordinary algorithms with comparable data access and hardware.

milestones.label: A predefined task family tested as inputs double
milestones.explanation: A benchmark family and its output, accuracy, success rate and data-handling rules would have to be fixed before testing successively doubled inputs. This would make the comparison well defined.

milestones.label: Complete costs and a precisely stated growing advantage
milestones.explanation: Runtime, energy and hardware would have to include every stage and state how many uses share setup costs. The claimed advantage must grow faster than any fixed power of input size in a named resource measure.

milestones.label: An advantage against the strongest matched ordinary algorithms
milestones.explanation: The quantum system would have to beat the strongest parallel ordinary algorithms with comparable hardware and access, including sampling weighted by squared data values where applicable. This would establish a fair advantage.

milestones.label: Reproducible results backed by an analysis of scaling
milestones.explanation: Independent reproduction and a scaling analysis would have to include physical data access and error-management costs. Measurements across a finite range alone cannot establish the required growth in advantage.

milestones.label: Clear limits on where the advantage holds
milestones.explanation: Results would have to state dataset sizes, errors, outputs, hardware needs and when the advantage appears or disappears. This would define which problems the demonstrated capability actually covers.

uncertain: It remains open whether any memory design and algorithm can preserve the required advantage after all physical costs and classical competition.
The benchmark family, accuracy target, resource measure and classical hardware budget remain to be chosen.
The physical obstacles facing proposed quantum memory designs have not been proved unavoidable.

page.title: End-to-end superpolynomial quantum speedup on classical data
page.definition: A quantum hardware workflow processes a specified family of classical datasets with a runtime advantage growing faster than every fixed power of the stated classical problem-size parameter. The comparison includes data loading, control, error management and answer extraction, against the best available classical algorithms with comparable access and hardware resources.

goal.need: A mouse-brain dataset records the activity of about 30,000 genes across 1.3 million cells. Biologists use patterns of variation in these measurements to distinguish cell types. Classical methods can process cells as they arrive, but merging genes to fit memory can obscure those patterns. On some changing data streams, a quantum method needs fewer observations than any classical method within a stated memory budget to locate a cell along a stable pattern. Whether this saves time on real cell data, including loading the observations and reading the answer, remains open.

statements.context: The statement concerns quantum machine learning, including a theoretical classification algorithm receiving classical inputs.

completion.title: A classical-data hardware computation retains a superpolynomial end-to-end runtime advantage.
completion.criterion: For a specified classical-data problem family, define size n in classical input units and match accuracy and success probability. Execute the complete hardware workflow and establish T_C(n)/T_Q(n)=n^{ω(1)} against the best available applicable classical algorithms. Include preparation, loading, access, classical control, error management, repetitions and requested-output extraction. Count preprocessing and its amortization on both sides. Match data access and hardware budgets, allowing classical parallelism. Establish asymptotic physical costs as well as measured performance; finite timings alone cannot establish this scaling.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no external document located specifies this combined completion test.
completion.basis: The IPAM programme describes a proof against the best possible classical algorithm as an ideal. The hardware test uses the best available classical algorithm, so a faster classical method can change the verdict. The ratio must grow faster than every fixed power of the stated classical input size. For example, N/polylog(N) is at most polynomial in N even though it grows exponentially in log N.

milestones.title: A quantum processor solves 2×2 linear systems using four qubits and four controlled gates.
milestones.criterion: Use four photonic qubits and four controlled gates to implement every subroutine of the published 2×2 linear-system circuit. For each of the protocol’s three input vectors, reconstruct the output density matrix from Pauli measurements and calculate its fidelity with the ideal solution state.
milestones.set_by: Cai et al., published experimental protocol; this benchmark concerns the linear-system case.
milestones.threshold_quote: We use four quantum bits and four controlled logic gates to implement every subroutine required

milestones.title: A classical-data task has efficiently generated instances with an expected, verifiable quantum advantage.
milestones.criterion: Give an efficient procedure for generating instances and specify how each algorithm accesses their classical data. Show why the quantum algorithm is expected to outperform the best known classical methods on the generated instances. Specify how a classical or quantum verifier can efficiently check the answer.
milestones.set_by: Google Quantum AI authors' proposed application-maturity framework, Stage II; a published framework, not a consensus standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: expected to exhibit verifiable quantum advantage

milestones.title: A classical-data quantum algorithm compiles to a complete set of physical machine instructions.
milestones.criterion: Compile a selected classical-data algorithm into executable physical instructions, including routing, error correction and non-Clifford resources. Obtain physical resource counts with the framework's stated allowance for uncertainty from decoding feedback. This reaches Stage IV(d), beyond compilation only to logical gates.
milestones.set_by: Google Quantum AI authors' proposed application-maturity framework, Stage IV(d).

milestones.title: A complete classical-data quantum workflow beats classical alternatives in total wall-clock time.
milestones.criterion: At matched accuracy and success probability, a physical classical-data workflow has T_C/T_Q>1 in total wall-clock time against the best available applicable classical algorithms. Include input preparation, loading, control, error management, repetitions and output extraction, with comparable hardware resources. This establishes an advantage over the tested sizes; it does not establish superpolynomial scaling.
milestones.set_by: Rønnow et al., published best-available-algorithm and wall-clock comparison conventions, applied to classical-data workflows.
milestones.threshold_quote: by comparing to the best available classical algorithm instead of the best possible classical algorithm.

milestones.title: A classical-data algorithm compiles to fault-tolerant operations for a specified architecture.
milestones.criterion: Map the algorithm’s logical gate circuit to fault-tolerant operations for a specified error-correcting architecture. Use that architecture’s cost model, including code distances and cycle times, to estimate the physical qubits and runtime for the chosen instance.
milestones.set_by: Google Quantum AI authors’ proposed application-maturity framework, Stage IV(c).
milestones.threshold_quote: Compilation to logical Quantum Error Correction (QEC) primitives.

milestones.title: A specific real-world task retains an expected quantum speedup after its overheads are included.
milestones.criterion: Identify a practical problem whose classical inputs and requested output match instances with an expected quantum advantage. Account for the application’s accuracy requirements, data access, output extraction and other overheads, and show why the remaining speedup would matter for that use.
milestones.set_by: Google Quantum AI authors’ proposed application-maturity framework, Stage III.
milestones.threshold_quote: a meaningful speedup, after accounting for all real-world constraints and overheads

not_found: No published external completion threshold combining classical-data input, superpolynomial scaling and demonstrated full hardware costs was located.
No quantitative dataset-size cutoff for large classical data was found in the searched frameworks and benchmarking documents.

results.finding: Sparse polynomial eigenvalue transforms on N×N matrices with at most d nonzeros per row have a potential Õ(√(Nd)) speedup in the medium-scale model.
results.detail: The comparison assumes a two-dimensional nearest-neighbour classical mesh and ignores signal latency. It uses a modeled cost comparison between QRAM access and classical matrix-vector multiplication.
results.quote: Thus, we have a square-root time advantage for the QRAM in this case.

results.finding: For m × n matrices, classical low-rank row sampling incurs at most a polynomial slowdown in the stated comparison.
results.detail: The comparison assumes the matrix is already stored in the shared data structure. The classical runtime has polynomial dependence on inverse sampling error, while the cited quantum runtime has logarithmic dependence.
results.quote:
As a
consequence, Kerenidis and Prakash’s algorithm does not in fact give an exponential
speedup over classical algorithms.

results.finding: For m users and n products, classical recommendation sampling runs in O(poly(k, 1/ε) polylog(mn)) time.
results.detail: The guarantee assumes a nearly low-rank preference matrix and access to a constant fraction of its entries through a prebuilt data structure. The paper describes that data coverage requirement as impractical.
results.quote: with probability 1 − (mn)−Θ(1) in O(poly(k, 1/ε) polylog(mn)) time.

results.detail: Classical soundness depends on the subexponential knowledge-of-lattice-point and adaptive-hardcore-bit assumptions. The paper gives partial evidence for the carry-predicate assumption.

results.finding: For one RSA-2048 factoring configuration, the compiled Pinnacle 1 circuit requires an estimated 48,000 physical qubits.
results.detail: The best listed estimate uses code distance 10, a physical error rate of 10⁻⁴ and a 1 µs code cycle. Runtime is modeled using compiled instruction timings and simulated logical error rates.

results.finding: For one RSA-2048 factoring task, Pinnacle 1.2 streamed the complete fault-tolerant instruction sequence for model validation.

results.quote: We validate the compiled circuit against models of the relevant Pinnacle 1 instantiations by streaming the complete sequence of instructions required for factoring and verifying that each satisfies the architecture’s constraints.

results.finding: Across four industrial models, simulated Iterative-QAOA partitions cut LS-DYNA runtime by up to 14.6% versus LS-GPart.
results.detail: The Drill benchmark ran two transient timesteps. The production estimate assumes that one ordering can be reused across many solves and that the measured saving persists.
results.quote: Further benchmarks using the NVIDIA CUDA-Q/cuTensorNet MPS simulator yielded a maximum WCT reduction of about 14.6% for the Drill model, 13.8% for the JetEngine model, 9.7% for the Impeller model, and 5.9% for the SedanCar model.

results.finding: Across three Forte-tested models, the best hardware-derived Drill partition cut LS-DYNA wall-clock time by about 12% versus LS-GPart.
results.detail: The reported gain selects the best of 20 shortlisted partitions. At the smallest coarse graph sizes, median partitions offered little or no gain. The study leaves a same-pipeline comparison with a classical coarse-graph solver for future work.
results.quote: In hardware executions on the IonQ Forte QPU utilizing 36-node coarse graphs, we observed a WCT reduction of about 12% for the Drill model, with more modest improvements for the Impeller and SedanCar.

results.finding: For L-bit integer inputs, Shor derives O(L² log L log log L) quantum steps for factoring with polynomial-time classical post-processing.
results.detail: The runtime result is theoretical and has no empirical sample. Choosing a random base modulo an already supplied integer is a step inside the factoring algorithm.
results.quote:
These algorithms take a number of
steps polynomial in the input size, e.g., the number of digits of the
integer to be factored.

results.finding: D-Wave Advantage showed an estimated 15× wall-clock advantage over tested classical heuristics on 50 hardware-native CBFM-P Ising instances with 5,387 variables each.
results.detail: The comparison used observed objective values and interpolated classical runtimes where needed. Hardware-native inputs bypassed encoding and embedding. Most classical solvers in the main comparison ran single-threaded.
results.quote:
In particular, the estimated
\(15 \times \)
run time ratio for the largest problem size is encouraging, as this suggests that the solutions identified by the QPU, even when accessed via a cloud computing service, can be obtained quickly enough to accelerate the performance of classical heuristic methods.

results.finding: Factoring one 2048-bit RSA integer is estimated to require fewer than one million physical qubits on a fault-tolerant surface-code architecture.
results.detail: The author budgets about 100,000 extra qubits for layout and scheduling slack. Detailed simulation of how cold-storage parity checks interact with lookup traffic remains pending.

goal.need = "A mouse-brain dataset records the activity of about 30,000 genes across 1.3 million cells. Biologists use patterns of variation in these measurements to distinguish cell types. Classical methods can process cells as they arrive, but merging genes to fit memory can obscure those patterns. On some changing data streams, a quantum method needs fewer observations than any classical method within a stated memory budget to locate a cell along a stable pattern. Whether this saves time on real cell data, including loading the observations and reading the answer, remains open.". Reason: The current rationale gives algorithm comparisons without showing who needs the computation, what they could learn, or why a memory advantage may fail to save time.
